problem: Hierarchical topometric maps are efficient but lack object-level semantics, while 3D scene graphs are semantically rich but computationally heavy. Existing semantic planners use only a single semantic layer (objects or rooms), not both.
motivation: Semantic navigation needs maps that balance computational efficiency with semantic richness. Planning over both fine-grained (object) and coarse-grained (room) semantics could make paths more meaningful and cheaper to compute, and support goals such as objects that are not yet on the map.
key_idea: Build a three-layer (metric, object, room) hierarchical semantic topometric map (IntelliMap) and plan on its semantic graph with Dijkstra, using an LLM to guess likely rooms for objects that are not on the map.
insight: Combining object-level and room-level semantics in one graph lets planning run in milliseconds (average 7 ms, max 10 ms over 50 tests) on a lightweight graph. The LLM-based discovery mode is much weaker (55% success) than known-target planning (99%), so LLM room-guessing is the bottleneck. There are no ablations, and the only comparison with prior work is a qualitative feature table.
method: IntelliMap framework: metric SLAM, Object Mapping, Room Segmentation and Place Categorization (ontology- or LLM-based) produce a metric-semantic map and a topological-semantic map, which are merged into a hierarchical topometric map.

Three-layer map: a Metric layer (costmap/octomap/grid), an Object layer (objects with pose) and a Room layer (segmented and categorized rooms). This is stored as a graph with object nodes, room nodes, room-connectivity edges and object-in-room edges.
Semantic planning graph: nodes are rooms and objects, and edges are weighted by distance, time or energy.
Targeted Navigation Mode: if the goal exists as a single node in the map, run Dijkstra from the start to it.
Multi-target Exploration Mode: if the goal matches several nodes, run Dijkstra to each and pick the shortest path.
Discovery Mode: if the goal object is not in the map, ChatGPT-3.5 is given the room attributes and returns the likely room(s), then Dijkstra plans to them.

setting.backbone: ChatGPT 3.5 (frozen, only for discovery mode) + Dijkstra graph search
setting.observation: Camera RGB (optionally LiDAR/IMU) via metric SLAM; the demo uses the uHumans2 Unity office dataset
setting.action_space: Graph node path (sequence of rooms/objects) over a costmap-based semantic graph
setting.privileged: Not stated; the semantic map appears to be built ahead of planning and is given to the planner

numbers_note: No standard benchmark. Only planner runtime and success rate over 50 tests in one simulated office are reported, in text, so they are not entered as benchmark rows. Those figures are: average time 7 ms, max 10 ms, 99% success for known targets and 55% for goal discovery.
results: In 50 tests in a simulated office, planning to known targets took 7 ms on average (10 ms max) with 99% success. Goal-discovery via ChatGPT-3.5 succeeded 55% of the time. A qualitative feature table shows IntelliMove as the only method covering all of the metric, object, room, object-based-planning and room-based-planning features.
limitations: Evaluation is minimal: one simulated office, 50 tests, no baseline comparison of planning performance and no standard benchmark.
Discovery mode reaches only 55% success and relies on a frozen LLM's room guesses, with no exploration or verification.
Planning is on a static graph; dynamic adaptation is claimed but not evaluated, and there is no real-robot test.
